summary.text: Alexander the Great was king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon from 336 BC until his death in 323 BC.
He invaded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in 334 BC, and by the age of 30 he had created one of the largest empires in history.
His conquests spread Greek culture as far east as the Indian subcontinent, and his death marks the conventional beginning of the Hellenistic period.

facts.label: Reign
facts.value: King of Macedon from 336 BC until 323 BC

facts.label: Teacher
facts.value: Tutored by Aristotle until the age of 16

facts.value: More than twenty, most prominently Alexandria in Egypt

facts.value: Mutiny from his troops forced him back at the Beas River

items.prompt: Alexander had beaten an Indian king and wanted to push on toward the ends of the world. What forced him to turn back?

options.label: A defeat at the hands of the Indian king
Persian armies cutting off his road home
His own troops threatened to rebel
A revolt in Thebes that needed his return

items.explain: Facing mutiny from his troops, he was forced to turn back at the Beas River after the victory over Porus.

items.prompt: In the years after Alexander died, what happened to his empire?

options.label: Civil wars broke out and it broke apart under the Diadochi
The League of Corinth reunited it under Greek rule
His heir ruled it peacefully for generations
Persia quickly won back all its old territory

items.explain: A series of civil wars broke across the empire, leading to its disintegration at the hands of the Diadochi.

items.prompt: A merchant far from Greece finds Greek used as a common language and Greek-style cities all around. What best explains this?

options.label: Greek armies had ruled the region for centuries before
Persian rulers had adopted Greek as their court language
Trade alone had spread Greek with no new cities
Conquests by a Macedonian king planted Greek colonies and culture

items.explain: Alexander founded more than twenty cities and spread Greek colonies and culture, so Greek became the lingua franca of the region.

items.prompt: Everyone gave up on a horse that refused to be mounted. At ten, young Alexander asked to try. What had he noticed?

options.label: The horse had an injured leg
The horse was afraid of its own shadow
The horse had been mistreated by its trader
The horse wanted a lighter rider

items.explain: Alexander detected the horse's fear of its own shadow and eventually managed to tame it.

items.prompt: Stories say a famous temple burned down on the day Alexander was born because a goddess was away. Why might such legends have arisen?

options.label: They may have spread in his reign to show he was destined for greatness
They were official records kept by Philip's court
They arose centuries later with no link to his reign
They were told by Aristotle to teach history to his pupils

items.explain: Such legends may have emerged while Alexander was king, possibly at his instigation, to show he was superhuman and destined for greatness.

items.prompt: After Alexander's victories at Issus and Gaugamela, what happened to the Persian king's empire?

options.label: It gave up Asia Minor but kept Mesopotamia
It was split between him and the Persian king
Its power was broken and he went on to conquer all of it
It became his ally and kept its own army

items.explain: After decisive battles at Issus and Gaugamela the power of the Achaemenid Empire was broken, and he conquered it entirely.

paragraphs.heading: King of Macedon
paragraphs.text: Alexander III of Macedon, known as Alexander the Great, was king of Macedon, an ancient Greek kingdom, from 336 BC to his death in 323 BC. He was the son of Philip II and of Olympias, Philip's fourth wife, and he took the throne at 20 after his father was assassinated. He spent most of his reign at war across Asia and Egypt, and by 30 he had built one of the largest empires in history, reaching from Greece to northwestern India. He never lost a battle, and many rank him among the greatest military commanders of all time.

paragraphs.heading: Growing up
paragraphs.text: He was born in Pella in Macedon. As a small child he was cared for by a nurse named Lanike, and later he was taught by tutors including the strict Leonidas. The philosopher Aristotle also taught him until he was 16. Like other young Macedonian nobles, he learned to read, play the lyre, ride, fight and hunt. When he was ten, a trader offered Philip a horse that refused to be mounted; Alexander saw that it feared its own shadow and managed to tame it, and Plutarch reports that Philip told him to find a kingdom big enough for his ambitions.

paragraphs.heading: Legends of his birth
paragraphs.text: Many stories grew up around his birth. Plutarch tells that just before her marriage was consummated, Olympias dreamed a thunderbolt struck her womb and sent a flame spreading far and wide. Another tale said the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus burned down on the day he was born, because the goddess was away attending his birth. Such legends may have started once he was king, possibly at his own urging, to show he was more than human from the start.

paragraphs.heading: Conquering Persia
paragraphs.text: Soon after becoming king, in 335 BC, he campaigned in the Balkans and then marched on Thebes, which was destroyed. He next took charge of the League of Corinth, which his father had created. Using that authority over the Greeks, he invaded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in 334 BC, starting ten years of campaigns. After taking Asia Minor and winning key battles at Issus and Gaugamela, he overthrew Darius III and conquered the whole Persian empire, so that his realm stretched from the Adriatic Sea to the Indus River.

paragraphs.heading: India and the end
paragraphs.text: Hoping to reach the ends of the world, he invaded India in 326 BC and beat Porus, an Indian king, at the Battle of the Hydaspes. But his troops mutinied, and he was forced to turn back at the Beas River. On the way home he died in 323 BC in Babylon, the city he had planned to make his capital, so his intended invasion of Arabia never came. Civil wars then tore his empire apart at the hands of the Diadochi, and his death is the usual starting point of the Hellenistic period.

paragraphs.heading: A lasting legacy
paragraphs.text: He founded more than twenty cities, the best known being Alexandria in Egypt. The Greek colonies he set up spread Greek culture so widely that Hellenistic civilization became a major force, felt as far east as the Indian subcontinent. Cultures mixed in his wake, giving rise to Greco-Buddhism and Hellenistic Judaism. Greek became the shared language of the region and stayed the main language of the Byzantine Empire until it fell in 1453 AD.

paragraphs.heading: Hero and legend
paragraphs.text: Alexander became a legendary hero, much like Achilles, in Greek and non-Greek traditions alike. Later generals measured themselves against his record, and military academies around the world still study his tactics. Stories about him were gathered in the 3rd century into the Alexander Romance, which was translated into almost every European language and every language of the Islamic world. Before modern times, only the Bible was more popular as European literature.
